New machine. Its objects are: lupuze, dosikas, vuvepo, zokapun, zavafan, ziludak.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: lupuze, dosikas, vuvepo
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first three objects together did not light the machine, but I don't yet know the rule. If any single nexiom is enough to light it, then lupuze, dosikas and vuvepo are all ruled out. That would leave the pair somewhere among zokapun, zavafan and ziludak. If both nexioms are needed together, many more pairs are still possible.

Testing zokapun on its own helps either way. Under the "any one is enough" rule, it tells me whether zokapun is one of the pair. If it doesn't light, the pair would be zavafan and ziludak. Under the "both needed" rule, a single object should never light the machine, so this result also helps check which rule applies.

TEST: zokapun
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Two tests have failed to light the machine: lupuze, dosikas and vuvepo together, then zokapun alone. I still don't know the rule, so I'll consider three.

- **Any one nexiom lights it:** the first failure rules out lupuze, dosikas and vuvepo. Zokapun failing alone rules it out too. The pair would have to be zavafan and ziludak.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** the failures only show the pair isn't contained in the first three objects. Many pairs are still possible.
- **Exactly one nexiom present lights it:** the first failure means that group held either zero or two nexioms. Zokapun is ruled out. So the pair is either two of lupuze, dosikas, vuvepo, or zavafan and ziludak.

Testing zavafan and ziludak together separates these cases. If it lights, only the first two rules fit, and both point to zavafan and ziludak. If it doesn't light, the "any one" rule is gone and zavafan plus ziludak can't be the pair under "both needed". I'd then have one test left for the remaining cases.

TEST: zavafan, ziludak
Result: the machine LIT UP. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

The three results point to one pair under every simple rule I considered:

- **Any one nexiom lights it:** lupuze, dosikas, vuvepo and zokapun all failed to light it, so they are ruled out. The pair is zavafan and ziludak, which fits their lighting up together.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** zavafan and ziludak lit up together, so the pair must be exactly those two.
- **Exactly one nexiom present lights it:** this rule no longer fits. The lit test would mean only one of zavafan and ziludak is a nexiom. Zokapun is ruled out, so the other nexiom would be among lupuze, dosikas and vuvepo. The first test would then have contained exactly one nexiom and lit up, but it didn't.

An unusual inverted rule (lighting only when no nexiom is present) would still fit. My last test couldn't fully settle that case, so I'll answer now.

ANSWER: nexioms = zavafan, ziludak
One last question. If only zavafan were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

I can't be sure, because my tests never separated the two rules that fit the results.

- **Any one nexiom lights it:** zavafan alone would light the machine.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** zavafan alone would not light it.

Every result so far fits both rules equally well. Zokapun failing alone is expected either way, since it isn't a nexiom. Zavafan and ziludak lighting together is also expected either way. Testing zavafan alone as my last move would have settled this. I chose to answer instead, so this is a guess.

I lean slightly toward the rule that both nexioms are needed, so my guess is that it would not light up.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: zezefok, nevevan, goduza, dovorek, forivak, lofove.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: zezefok, nevevan, goduza
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first test didn't light up with zezefok, nevevan and goduza on the machine. If any single nexiom is enough to light it, both nexioms must be among dovorek, forivak and lofove. Testing dovorek alone checks that idea and helps narrow down the pair.

TEST: dovorek
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

The first two tests didn't light up, but I still don't know the machine's rule. Putting forivak and lofove on together is informative under several possible rules:
- **Any one nexiom lights it:** both nexioms must be among dovorek, forivak and lofove, and dovorek is ruled out, so the pair should be forivak and lofove. The machine should light.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** it lights only if the pair is exactly forivak and lofove.
- **Exactly one nexiom lights it:** it can't light, because the first test rules out a split pair with one of them among zezefok, nevevan and goduza.

So if it lights, the answer should be forivak and lofove. If it doesn't, I'll use my last test to narrow things down.

TEST: forivak, lofove
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

After three tests where the machine never lit, the simplest rule is ruled out. The rule "any one nexiom lights it" is impossible. It would make forivak and lofove the pair, but they didn't light together.

Two rules still fit the results:
- **Exactly one nexiom lights it:** dovorek is not a nexiom. The pair is forivak and lofove, or two of zezefok, nevevan and goduza.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** any pair still fits except two from zezefok, nevevan and goduza, or forivak and lofove. That leaves 11 possible pairs.

One test can't settle all of this, so I'll split the "exactly one" options. Testing zezefok alone:
- **If it lights:** the pair is zezefok with nevevan or with goduza.
- **If it doesn't:** the likely pairs are nevevan and goduza, or forivak and lofove.

TEST: zezefok
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

No test lit the machine. Rules that light whenever any one nexiom is present are ruled out. That leaves two rules:
- **Exactly one nexiom lights it:** the pair must be forivak and lofove, or nevevan and goduza. Each of these pairs never had just one member on the machine in any test, so they fit all four results equally well.
- **Both nexioms are needed:** many pairs still fit, but not these two. Each was on the machine together without lighting it.

The tests couldn't separate these possibilities, so this answer is a guess. I'm choosing one of the two "exactly one" candidates.

ANSWER: nexioms = forivak, lofove
One last question. If only forivak were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

Under the reading behind my answer, the machine lights when exactly one nexiom is on it, and the nexioms are forivak and lofove. Forivak alone would then be exactly one nexiom, so the machine should light.

This is not certain. If the real rule is that both nexioms are needed, forivak alone would not light it. If forivak is not a nexiom at all, it would not light either.

PROBE: yes

New machine. Its objects are: doveda, lutufur, detamo, milaren, letanun, salozer.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to see how the machine responds.

TEST: doveda, lutufur, detamo
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

Under an "any nexiom lights it" rule, both nexioms would have to be among the other three. Under a "both nexioms needed" rule, the first group simply didn't contain both. Testing the other three objects should help tell these apart.

TEST: milaren, letanun, salozer
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Neither half lit up, so the machine can't be lighting whenever at least one nexiom is present. The most likely rule is that both nexioms must be on the machine together. That would mean one nexiom is among doveda, lutufur and detamo, and the other is among milaren, letanun and salozer. That leaves 9 candidate pairs.

Two yes/no tests can only separate 4 groups, so I can't be certain of the pair. I'll narrow it as much as I can. This test lights up only if the nexioms are one of doveda or lutufur together with one of milaren or letanun.

TEST: doveda, lutufur, milaren, letanun
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Under the "both nexioms needed" rule, five pairs are still possible:
- detamo with milaren
- detamo with letanun
- detamo with salozer
- doveda with salozer
- lutufur with salozer

One test can only split these into two groups, so I can't be certain of the final pair. This test lights up only if the pair is detamo with milaren or detamo with letanun. If it doesn't light up, the pair must include salozer.

TEST: detamo, milaren, letanun
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

I can't be sure of the pair; this is a one-in-three guess.

The evidence, assuming the machine lights only when both nexioms are on it:
- **First two tests:** neither half lit up, so one nexiom is among doveda, lutufur and detamo, and the other is among milaren, letanun and salozer.
- **Third test:** this ruled out every pair made of doveda or lutufur with milaren or letanun.
- **Fourth test:** this ruled out detamo with milaren and detamo with letanun.

So one nexiom must be salozer. The other could be detamo, doveda or lutufur, and nothing I tested separates these three. I'm picking detamo.

My earlier test choices also had a flaw. Two yes/no results could never pin down one of nine pairs. Testing smaller groups early would also have checked the "both needed" rule itself, which I've only assumed.

ANSWER: nexioms = detamo, salozer
One last question. If only detamo were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**No**, detamo alone would not light the machine.

Non-nexioms never affect the machine. My best guess is that the nexioms are detamo and salozer, which makes milaren and letanun non-nexioms. The fourth test (detamo, milaren, letanun) is then effectively detamo on its own, and it did not light up.

This also fits the rule I've been assuming, that both nexioms must be present, since one object alone can't satisfy it. The "no" holds under other explanations too. For example, the rule might be "exactly one nexiom lights it," with doveda and lutufur as the nexioms. Then detamo isn't a nexiom at all and still wouldn't light the machine.

PROBE: no

New machine. Its objects are: zipeser, mikenir, betala, nefiga, luvota, sabune.
You have 4 tests. Make your first move.

I'll start by testing half of the objects to narrow down where the nexioms are.

TEST: zipeser, mikenir, betala
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 3 tests left. Make your next move.

The first test (zipeser, mikenir, betala) did not light up, so the nexioms are probably not both in that group. One possible rule is that the machine lights when any nexiom is present. If so, both nexioms are among nefiga, luvota and sabune. Testing nefiga alone shows whether it is one of them.

TEST: nefiga
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 2 tests left. Make your next move.

Two tests have failed: zipeser, mikenir and betala together, and nefiga alone. I still don't know the machine's rule. If it lights whenever any nexiom is present, then the nexioms must be luvota and sabune. If it needs both nexioms present, testing luvota and sabune together also checks whether they are the pair. So testing them together is informative under both rules.

TEST: luvota, sabune
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have 1 test left. Make your next move.

Here is what the three failed tests rule out:
- **"Lights if any nexiom is present"** is impossible. Every object has now been in a test that failed, so neither nexiom could be anywhere.
- **"Lights only if no nexiom is present"** is also impossible. Each of the three tests would need its own nexiom, which makes three.

Two rules still fit, each with its own candidate pairs:
- **"Lights only if both nexioms are present":** the pair is not inside {zipeser, mikenir, betala} and is not luvota + sabune. That leaves 11 possible pairs.
- **"Lights if exactly one nexiom is present":** the pair is inside {zipeser, mikenir, betala} or is luvota + sabune. That leaves 4 possible pairs.

One test cannot settle all of this, so I'll use a group of four that splits the candidates under both rules.

TEST: zipeser, mikenir, nefiga, luvota
Result: the machine did NOT light up. You have used all your tests. Give your ANSWER now.

I can't be sure, because the four tests leave seven equally likely pairs. Zipeser and mikenir is one guess among them.

**What the earlier tests ruled out:**
- **"Lights if any nexiom is present"** is impossible. Every object has been in a test that failed.
- **"Lights only if no nexiom is present"** is also impossible. The three separate failed groups would each need a nexiom, which makes three.

**What the last failed test (zipeser, mikenir, nefiga, luvota) leaves under the two remaining rules:**
- **"Lights only if both nexioms are present":** the pair cannot sit inside that test group. Six pairs remain:
  - betala + nefiga
  - betala + luvota
  - betala + sabune
  - sabune + zipeser
  - sabune + mikenir
  - sabune + nefiga
- **"Lights if exactly one nexiom is present":** the last test held zero or two nexioms. Of the four earlier candidates, only zipeser + mikenir fits.

**Choosing:** each of the seven pairs fits the results with the same likelihood. If the two rules are equally likely to begin with, every pair has about a 1 in 7 chance. Zipeser and mikenir is the only pair under the "exactly one" rule; the other six all depend on the "both" rule.

ANSWER: nexioms = zipeser, mikenir
One last question. If only mikenir were on the machine, with nothing else, would it light up? End your message with one line: PROBE: yes or PROBE: no

**Probably not, though this conflicts with my final answer, so my reasoning should be laid out.**

**If my answer (zipeser + mikenir) is right:** the only rule that fits that pair is "lights if exactly one nexiom is present." Mikenir alone would be exactly one nexiom, so the machine **would** light up.

**But that is the less likely case.** Seven pairs fit the results with roughly equal odds:
- **Zipeser + mikenir** fits only under the "exactly one" rule. That is about a 1 in 7 chance.
- **The other six pairs** fit under the "both nexioms present" rule. That is about a 6 in 7 chance. Under that rule, no single object can ever light the machine, so mikenir alone would **not** light it up.

Overall, "no" has about a 6 in 7 chance and "yes" about 1 in 7. I picked zipeser + mikenir because it was a single pair that is as likely as any other pair. But the "both" rule is more likely as a rule overall, and under it mikenir alone fails.

PROBE: no
